Medical Neuroanatomy · Chapter 5, The Pons · Case Study 5-1

The Man Who Couldn't Look Left

A 55-year-old man with sudden dysarthria, left facial weakness, and right hemiparesis — a crossed brainstem syndrome, worked up from the bedside exam outward.

● Localization ● Exam Finding ● Terminology ● Pattern Recognition ● Risk / Workup / Trajectory

Chief Complaint

A 55-year-old right-handed man was brought to the emergency room by his wife because of the sudden onset of slurred speech1 and extreme difficulty in walking.

History of Chief Complaint

He had experienced several episodes of weakness over a two-day period2 prior to his presentation. On the morning of his presentation he experienced a sudden onset of weakness and had fallen in the bathroom. He was unable to get up without his wife's assistance. Once he was upright, he found that his right leg felt very weak and dragged slightly3 as he attempted to walk. He also found that his right arm would not support him as he attempted to lean on the wall. He also complained of difficulty looking to the left4, but he denies any double vision5. His wife stated that the left side of his face looked different6.

Medical History

The patient was a professional accountant involved in management. He was married, with three children, one of whom was still living with him. He had enjoyed good health except for elevated blood pressure since turning 45 years of age7. He had a 10-pack-year history of smoking8 but quit all smoking at age 47. He is currently taking no medication.

Family History

His father died at 52 from cardiovascular disease9 and his mother at 49 from breast cancer. He has a 57-year-old brother who had coronary artery bypass surgery at age 53.

General Physical Examination

This was a stable, alert, oriented, cooperative, male, appearing his stated age and reclining in bed. He demonstrated appropriate concern about his condition. He had an asymmetric facial expression. His eyes were clear with no papilledema; his chest was clear to auscultation and percussion; his respirations and temperature were normal. His blood pressure was 193/9810 and pulse rate was 90. Peripheral pulses were present at the wrists but absent bilaterally at the ankles11. His abdomen was soft with no signs of tenderness or masses; a large scar in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen was residual from an old appendectomy. His skin was soft and warm, with normal turgor.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status

The patient was alert, oriented for person, place and time, and cooperative. His speech was dysarthric but fluent12. Memory, language, and comprehension were intact13. He could follow three-step commands. He gave a coherent history.

Cranial Nerves

There was no evidence of double vision, and his visual fields were intact to confrontation. His pupils were 3 to 4 mm in diameter and reactive to light14, both direct and consensual. The patient had volitional conjugate vision vertically in both directions and to the right, but not to the left15. Both eyes could be deflected to the left with the doll's head maneuver16. Convergence movements in both eyes were intact17. He had normal hearing (tested to finger rub) in both ears. His corneal reflex was present on the right but diminished on the left; however, brushing the left cornea was painful to him18. His facial expression was asymmetric. The left side of his mouth was open slightly and did not move when he spoke, his left eyelid would not shut as tightly as the right, and the wrinkles of the left side of the forehead were less pronounced than those on the right19. When he attempted to puff out his cheeks, air escaped from the left side of his mouth. The jaw-jerk and gag reflexes were intact20. His palate elevated along the midline.

Motor Systems

Strength was reduced in both extremities on the right compared to those on the left21. Tendon reflexes were elevated at the wrist, elbow, knee, and ankle on the right (+3/4)22 and were normal in all places in the left extremities. Plantar reflexes were extensor on the right and flexor on the left23. No past-pointing was present on the left, and finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin tests were normal for that extremity. He was unable to execute these tests with the right extremities. His right upper extremity was flexed at the elbow and resisted passive movement; his right lower extremity was extended and resisted flexion, even as he attempted to walk. Normal tone and station were present in the left limbs.

Sensation

Pinprick, light touch, and position and vibratory senses were intact throughout body and face24.

Follow-up

He remained in the hospital for 3 days and was discharged home with assistance from a day nurse. A re-evaluation done at 2.5 months post hospital discharge found almost complete recovery of gross motor strength25 in the right extremities with power at +4/5 for flexion and extension at the elbow, wrist, knee, and ankle. Grip strength was +4/5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. Deep tendon reflexes remained elevated at +3/4 at the elbow, wrist, knee and ankle. There was a very mild lack of coordination in the fine motor control of the right arm. Eye movements were complete in all fields. He had a mild residual facial asymmetry26 involving the area around his eye and his mouth.

Questions to Consider

  1. Has the patient experienced any changes in consciousness or cognition, language function or spatial recognition, personality or emotional behavior, or any loss in memory?
  2. Does the patient exhibit any loss of vision and if so, where in the visual field is the loss? Are there any visual hallucinations present in this patient?
  3. Are there any changes in cranial nerve function and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  4. Are there any changes in motor function such as reflexes, muscle tone, movement, or coordination and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  5. Are there any changes in sensory function and if so, what levels of the body have experienced this change?
  6. What is the clinical temporal profile of this patient's neurologic problem: is the onset of neurologic findings acute or insidious, and is the course of the neurologic disease chronically progressive, fluctuant or stable?
  7. Based on the presenting signs and symptoms, do you think the distribution of the neurologic pathology is focal, multifocal or diffuse?
  8. Based on the answers to these questions develop a differential diagnosis of the patient's neurological problem?
  9. If the origin of the pathology is vascular, what arterial supply is most likely involved with the lesion in this patient?

These are the original workbook questions. The Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough below works through them in order.

Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough

Localization → distribution → time course → differential → workup → prognosis → management

01 · Localization

A crossed brainstem syndrome

Left-sided cranial-nerve findings (a peripheral-type facial palsy — forehead, eye closure, and mouth all involved together — plus a horizontal gaze palsy without diplopia) are paired with right-sided long-tract findings (limb weakness, hyperreflexia, an extensor plantar response). That "crossed" pattern is the signature of a unilateral left pontine lesion: cranial-nerve fibers that haven't yet crossed the midline, alongside corticospinal fibers that also haven't crossed yet (they decussate lower, at the cervicomedullary junction). Three structures appear involved: the facial nucleus/nerve fascicle, the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) — note the doll's-head maneuver still moves the eyes left, which means the abducens nucleus itself is functionally intact and the deficit sits in the PPRF relay that drives it — and the corticospinal tract. Preserved sensation, intact vertical gaze, and reactive pupils keep this focal and tegmental, sparing the medial lemniscus, spinothalamic/trigeminal sensory pathways, and the midbrain.

02 · Distribution

Focal, unilateral

Everything localizes to one side of one structure — the left pons — in the territory of a single small paramedian perforating vessel, rather than to multifocal or diffuse disease. There is no evidence of bilateral, hemispheric, or multi-level involvement.

03 · Time Course

Acute, with a crescendo prodrome

Several transient episodes of weakness over the two days before presentation, culminating in a sudden, fixed deficit — a stepwise crescendo pattern rather than one single catastrophic event. This is the classic signature of in-situ branch (perforator) atherothrombotic disease, where a diseased small vessel narrows intermittently before finally occluding, rather than a single embolus arriving all at once.

04 · Differential Diagnosis

Working through the possibilities

DiagnosisFitsArgues Against
Basilar artery paramedian branch infarct
(pontine "Foville" tegmental syndrome)Most Likely		 Abrupt deficit after a 2-day crescendo of transient weakness; crossed left PPRF/CN VII + right corticospinal signs; dense vascular risk profile (hypertension, smoking history, absent ankle pulses, early-onset family cardiovascular disease); gradual, substantial recovery over weeks. None major — imaging is still needed to confirm territory and exclude hemorrhage.
Pontine hemorrhage Acute focal brainstem deficit; markedly elevated blood pressure (193/98) on presentation. Patient remained alert and cooperative throughout, without depressed consciousness or papilledema; the multi-day crescendo of transient episodes fits evolving ischemia better than a single hemorrhagic event.
Demyelinating plaque (e.g., MS) A single focal brainstem lesion can produce an isolated cranial-nerve-plus-long-tract picture. First neurologic event at age 55 is atypical for a new demyelinating attack; the dense vascular risk-factor burden makes an ischemic explanation far more likely.
Brainstem tumor / mass lesion Focal, structural-appearing signs referable to one side of the pons. Evolved over days, not weeks to months; no papilledema or other signs of mass effect; substantial early improvement argues against a persistent structural mass.
Bilateral ventral pontine infarction
(locked-in syndrome)		 Useful contrast case, not seriously entertained here. This patient is alert, fluent, and able to move his left face and right-sided limbs — nothing like the akinetic, mute, vertical-eye-movement-only picture of a bilateral ventral pontine lesion (see Concept Deep-Dive).

05 · Diagnostic Workup

What to order, and why

  1. 1Noncontrast CT head — first step for any acute deficit, to exclude hemorrhage before anything else.A pontine hemorrhage would change management immediately (no antiplatelets); a small paramedian ischemic infarct may not even be visible on CT.
  2. 2MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) — confirms and precisely localizes the acute infarct.DWI is far more sensitive than CT for small, acute posterior-fossa/brainstem infarcts, which are notoriously hard to see on CT due to bone artifact.
  3. 3MRA or CTA of the head and neck (vertebrobasilar system) — evaluates the basilar artery and its paramedian perforating branches.Looking for atherosclerotic narrowing or branch disease at the site implicated by the exam and MRI.
  4. 4ECG, telemetry, and echocardiogram — screens for a cardioembolic source.Even with a strong small-vessel story, an embolic contributor (e.g., atrial fibrillation) must be excluded, since it changes secondary-prevention therapy.
  5. 5Fasting lipid panel and glucose/HbA1c — completes the vascular risk-factor profile.Identifies additional modifiable targets (dyslipidemia, diabetes) alongside his known hypertension and smoking history.

06 · Prognosis

A generally favorable course

Small perforator-territory pontine infarcts carry a comparatively favorable prognosis, and this patient's own follow-up bears that out: by 2.5 months, right-extremity strength had recovered to nearly normal, though tendon reflexes stayed mildly hyperactive and a very mild fine-motor deficit persisted in the right arm. Eye movements normalized completely. The most durable finding was a mild residual facial asymmetry — a common long-term footprint of facial nucleus/nerve involvement, even once the motor tracts have substantially recovered.

07 · Management

Acute care → secondary prevention

  • Confirm ischemia vs. hemorrhage on imaging before any antithrombotic therapy; assess thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility (complicated here by the fluctuating, multi-day prodrome).
  • Permissive blood pressure management per acute ischemic stroke protocol, rather than aggressive early lowering (unless thrombolysis is given).
  • Antiplatelet therapy once hemorrhage is excluded; high-intensity statin.
  • Swallow evaluation given dysarthria/bulbar involvement, before resuming oral intake.
  • Eye protection for the left eye given incomplete lid closure, to prevent corneal exposure injury.
  • PT/OT/speech therapy for the right hemiparesis, fine-motor deficit, and dysarthria.
  • Long-term risk-factor control: blood pressure, glycemic and lipid management, smoking-relapse prevention.

Concept Deep-Dive

The pontine anatomy this case is actually testing

A note on scope: not everything below traces directly back to this case. Cards marked Aside capture things the professor brought up along the way — real teaching content, but tangents rather than findings from this patient's exam.

Localization

Three Lesions, One Question: Where's the Diplopia?

Working through it lesion by lesion: for each site, does the patient get diplopia, and does the doll's-head maneuver stay intact?

Working outward from the eye: a lesion of the abducens nerve (A/B) causes an isolated rectus palsy — one eye can't move while the other does, so the eyes point in different directions and the patient sees double. A lesion of the abducens nucleus (C) or of both MLFs (D/E, internuclear ophthalmoplegia) takes out conjugate movement itself, so the eyes stay yoked together and there's no diplopia — but the doll's-head maneuver is not intact, because the final common pathway to the muscle is damaged either way. Move one step further upstream, to the PPRF (G) or the frontal eye field (H), and something changes: diplopia is still absent, but now the doll's-head reflex is intact, because the vestibular route into the abducens nucleus (via CN VIII) bypasses the damaged relay entirely.

This patientHe is row G on this map: a left lateral gaze palsy, no diplopia, and an intact doll's-head reflex. That combination — and specifically the intact reflex — is what places the lesion at the PPRF rather than at the abducens nucleus itself (row C).
Pattern Recognition

Central vs. Peripheral Facial Palsy

Figure 5-4 — corticonuclear input to the facial nucleus: bilateral to the upper face, contralateral-dominant to the lower face.

The upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receives bilateral cortical innervation, so a one-sided cortical or corticonuclear lesion still leaves it working — only the contralateral lower face droops. The facial nucleus and nerve themselves, by contrast, drive the entire ipsilateral face; damage there takes out forehead, eye closure, and mouth together.

This patientHis left forehead wrinkles are diminished and his left eye won't close tightly — full hemifacial involvement, not just lower-face drooping. That's the signature of a peripheral/LMN-type palsy at the level of the facial nucleus or nerve, exactly where a left pontine lesion would strike it.
Exam Finding

Bedside: Testing the Facial Nerve, Top to Bottom

Top to bottom: wrinkle the forehead, shut the eyes against resistance, show the teeth, puff the cheeks.

The exam is run in order from the top of the face to the bottom, matching the facial nucleus's own top-to-bottom organization: raise the eyebrows/wrinkle the forehead, then shut the eyes as tightly as possible while the examiner tries to pry them open, then bare the teeth, then puff the cheeks — tapping on the puffed cheek and watching whether air leaks out is a way to catch a subtle asymmetry that isn't obvious just from looking.

This patientHe could not shut the left eye as tightly as the right and air escaped from the left corner of his mouth on puffing — both top and bottom involved, again pointing to a peripheral-type palsy.
Pattern Recognition

The Eyelash Sign: Catching a Subtle Weakness

Ask the patient to squeeze both eyes shut as hard as they can, then look closely at the eyelashes on each side. Normally the lashes get buried and become hard to see. On a weak side, even a subtle one, the lashes stay visible because the orbicularis oculi can't generate quite as much closing force. Because it's a side-to-side comparison on the same face, it can pick up a degree of weakness too mild to notice on gross inspection.

This patientThis is the same finding as his diminished forehead wrinkling and incomplete eye closure — different bedside tests converging on one conclusion: the left orbicularis oculi is weak.
Terminology

Why One Small Lesion Hits Three Systems

Figure 5-1 — the abducens nucleus and its radiations pass directly alongside the corticospinal fibers of the pyramidal tract (Py/CST), with the facial nucleus nearby.

In the caudal pons, the abducens nucleus sits in the dorsal tegmentum near the floor of the fourth ventricle, its radiations sweep ventrally right past the corticospinal fibers of the basis pontis, and the facial nucleus lies close by. Because these structures are packed so tightly together, a single small paramedian infarct in this territory can plausibly damage the gaze-control circuitry, the facial nucleus/fascicle, and the corticospinal tract all at once.

This patientThat anatomic crowding is exactly why one small vascular lesion produced three seemingly unrelated findings — a gaze palsy, a facial palsy, and a contralateral hemiparesis.
Localization

Doll's Eyes: The Reflex That Bypasses the Lesion

The vestibulo-ocular reflex reaches the abducens nucleus through vestibular nuclei and the MLF — bypassing the cortex and the PPRF entirely. Because this reflex still moves both eyes left, the abducens nucleus and its motor output must be functionally intact. That shifts the localization of the volitional gaze palsy specifically to the PPRF, the relay that carries the cortical gaze command into the nucleus, rather than to the nucleus itself.

This patientThe doll's-head maneuver is the single bedside test that separates "PPRF lesion" from "abducens nucleus lesion" — and here it points to the PPRF.
Localization

How the Reflex Actually Fires

Left: the full VOR arc — head rotation is sensed on both sides, and the signal is both crossed and uncrossed on its way to the eye muscles. Right: what the canal itself is doing — angular head acceleration displaces the cupula and bends the hair cells.

Turning the head to the left speeds up endolymph flow in the left horizontal canal and slows it in the right, so the left vestibular nucleus fires more than the right. From there the pathway splits: the left vestibular nucleus excites the contralateral (right) abducens nucleus directly, and that abducens nucleus sends a second signal up the MLF to the ipsilateral (left) oculomotor nucleus. The net result — right lateral rectus and left medial rectus contract together — is a fast, reflexive conjugate eye movement to the right, i.e. opposite the head turn, at a speed proportional to how fast the head moved.

This patientBecause this circuit runs canal → vestibular nucleus → abducens nucleus → MLF → oculomotor nucleus, it never touches the cortex or the PPRF. That's exactly why it still works when the voluntary gaze command doesn't.
Exam Finding

Bedside: Why the Maneuver Only Works Here

The general head-impulse principle: a healthy VOR keeps the eyes locked on target through a quick head turn.

This illustration is the standard way the VOR is tested — a healthy reflex keeps gaze fixed on the examiner through a fast head turn; a weak one lets the eyes drift with the head and needs a corrective saccade back. That's usually used to look for a vestibular problem. In this case the reflex itself isn't in question — it's being used as a diagnostic shortcut in the other direction: since a normal, conscious person can just override the doll's-head maneuver by fixating voluntarily, it "tells you nothing" unless the person truly cannot move their eyes into that field on command. That's exactly this patient's situation, so the maneuver becomes informative.

This patientHe's awake and cooperative, but because he can't voluntarily look left, the doll's-head test isn't overridden — it becomes a clean bypass that proves the final common pathway (nucleus, nerve, muscle) is intact.
Exam Finding

The Crossed Syndrome, Wired Out

Cranial-nerve fibers in the pons are still on their side of origin — a lesion there produces an ipsilateral deficit. Corticospinal fibers passing through the pons are also still uncrossed at this level, but they don't cross until the cervicomedullary junction much lower down — so the same lesion produces a contralateral body deficit.

This patientLeft face + right body is not two separate problems — it's the expected wiring diagram of a single left pontine lesion, sitting above the corticospinal decussation but at the level of the (uncrossed) facial and gaze pathways.
Workup / Vascular

Millard-Gubler vs. Foville: Naming This Syndrome

FeatureMillard-Gubler
(ventral pons)		Foville
(dorsal/tegmental pons)
Eye findingIsolated CN VI nerve palsy → diplopia on lateral gazePPRF/nucleus-level gaze palsy → no diplopia
Facial findingIpsilateral peripheral CN VII palsyIpsilateral peripheral CN VII palsy
Limb findingContralateral hemiparesisContralateral hemiparesis
This patient—✓ Matches

Both syndromes share the same "ipsilateral face, contralateral body" crossed pattern and arise from the same general vascular territory — paramedian branches of the basilar artery. What separates them is exactly the bedside detail this exam captured: whether the eye finding is a nerve-level palsy with diplopia (Millard-Gubler, more ventral) or a gaze-center palsy without diplopia and with a preserved doll's-head reflex (Foville, more dorsal/tegmental).

This patientNo diplopia + intact vestibulo-ocular reflex + peripheral facial palsy + contralateral hemiparesis = Foville syndrome, from a paramedian branch of the basilar artery — which is also the answer to the case's own Question 9.
Workup / Vascular

Naming the Vessel: Reading the Territory

A teaching cross-section of the caudal pons: the paramedian region (left circle, containing the abducens nucleus, PPRF, and facial nucleus) versus a more lateral territory (right circle).

The pons is supplied by three overlapping groups of vessels off the basilar artery: paramedian perforators, which dive straight in near the midline and supply exactly the dorsal tegmental structures circled here (abducens nucleus/PPRF, facial nucleus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, corticospinal fibers); short circumferential arteries, which wrap partway around to supply the lateral pons; and the long circumferential arteries — namely the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) and, more caudally, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) — which continue all the way around to the cerebellum.

This patientThe left circle above is this case: a single paramedian perforator occluded, taking out the PPRF/CN VI pathway, the facial nucleus, and the corticospinal tract together — exactly the vascular explanation for a syndrome that looks like three separate problems.
Workup / Vascular

The Same Territory, in Real Tissue

Plate 14 — an actual pontine cross-section, with the paramedian territory of the Medial (Caudal) Pontine Syndrome highlighted, for orientation against the diagrams above.

Diagrams simplify the pons into clean circles and labels; real tissue is messier, and being able to move between the two is a core neuroanatomy skill. This is the classic teaching plate for Medial (Caudal) Pontine Syndrome — occlusion of a paramedian perforator at the level of the abducens/facial nuclei. The highlighted wedge is small, medially placed, and disproportionately consequential because of how tightly the gaze, facial, and motor pathways are packed into it.

This patientA single small, unglamorous perforating vessel — not a large-territory stroke — accounts for the entire clinical picture, which is also why his prognosis for partial recovery was relatively good.
Aside

Not This Case, But Came Up: The Corticopontocerebellar Pathway

Cortex → corticopontine fibers → basilar pons (pontine nuclei) → pontocerebellar fibers → contralateral cerebellar cortex → dentate nucleus.

Near the end of this session the discussion drifted from Foville syndrome to a different pontine story: how the cerebral cortex talks to the cerebellum. Corticopontine fibers descend with the corticospinal tract, synapse on the pontine nuclei scattered through the basilar pons, and those neurons cross the midline as pontocerebellar fibers to enter the opposite cerebellar hemisphere through the middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) — which is why the MCP is so large: it's carrying the entire cortical "instruction set" for the contralateral cerebellum. This is also why cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the cerebellar lesion but referable to the contralateral cortex.

Not part of this patient's caseUseful background, but it belongs to a different pontine syndrome (cerebellar/ataxic presentations) — not to the paramedian infarct discussed here.
